claims.text: Ashish Rajan's article of 16 October opens with Northstar, a fictional retailer whose support agent may refund up to $200, a limit enforced by the payment service, not only written in the agent's instructions.
claims.quote: That limit is enforced by the payment service, not just written into the agent's instructions.

claims.text: A customer is entitled to $120, the agent misinterprets a discount and refunds $150, the payment service accepts it, and the logs are complete.
claims.quote: But the agent misinterprets a discount and calculates a refund of $150.

claims.text: The problem in one sentence: the system did what it was allowed to do, it just did not do what it was supposed to do.
claims.quote: The system did what it was allowed to do. It just didn't do what it was supposed to do.

claims.text: His answer, from AI Security Lab, is four questions: SECURE, OBSERVE, RESPOND and VERIFY, which he says are not four sequential stages and no one of which replaces the others.
claims.quote: not four sequential stages, and no single capability replaces the others.

claims.text: SECURE is answered by the Agent Behaviour Policy: each row names a capability, its reach and a mandate, and says what keeps it, an expectation, a setting or a boundary.
claims.quote: Each row names a capability, its reach, and a mandate: yes, no, or approval.

claims.text: In Hope or enforcement the same customer service agent built three ways went from 97% of its rules kept by hope to 23%, as the limits moved into the tools.
claims.quote: went from 97% of its rules kept by hope to 23%, as the limits moved into the tools.

value.unit: percent of rules kept by hope in the third design

claims.text: In the SGit and Ruflo run, Mondweep Chakravorty compiled an ABP into Ruflo's own rules and checked them in enforce mode, outside the agent.
claims.quote: compiled an ABP into Ruflo's own rules and checked them in enforce mode, outside the agent.

claims.text: A behaviour policy answers may it, and the question was is it right: a limit cannot tell $150 from $120 when both are under $200.
claims.quote: A limit cannot tell $150 from $120 when both are under $200.

claims.text: VERIFY needs an intended requirement written down first; for Northstar that is a rule, refund what was paid for the returned item after any discount less anything already refunded, and that is a decision policy.
claims.quote: someone has to have written down what right is, before anyone can prove it happened.

claims.text: An Agent Decision Policy says, at a branch point, who decides, on what evidence, within what limits, and who to call when it is out of bounds.
claims.quote: at a branch point, who decides, on what evidence, within what limits, and who to call when it is out of bounds.

claims.text: His example found a gap in the owner's own work: the refund scenario in three decisions, mapped was marked mature, yet below its 100 GBP limit nothing checked the amount, and the map now adds a fifth state, verified, beside observed.
claims.quote: Observed means we can reconstruct what happened; verified means we can prove it was right.

claims.text: His four questions cut across the three policies; VERIFY has nothing in the behaviour column, because a limit can only say what may be done.
claims.quote: VERIFY has nothing in the behaviour column, and I think it never will: a limit can only say what may be done.

claims.text: SECURE has a workflow cell: in the strongest design the agent proposes an amount, the decision policy decides, and the workflow pays the decided amount, so a wrong proposal is a recorded difference, not a payment.
claims.quote: A wrong proposal is then a recorded difference, not a payment.

claims.text: Northstar was built as a twin in an sgit vault: thirteen synthetic refund requests, each with something an agent can get wrong, run through four designs of the controls, every step replayable, nothing called live.
claims.quote: It has thirteen synthetic refund requests, each with something an agent can get wrong

claims.text: Design A, as described in the article, overpays $458 and leaves $341.60 owed, getting 1 of 13 cases right with no people's time.
claims.quote: The design in the article overpays $458 and leaves $341.60 owed.

claims.text: Design B, secure, observe and respond done well, stops most of the overpayment by refusing and leaves $222.60 owed across four customers.
claims.quote: B leaves $222.60 owed across four customers.

value.unit: USD still owed in design B

claims.text: Design C adds VERIFY and gets every amount right by sending every mismatch and uncovered case to a person: 57 minutes of people's time on thirteen refunds.
claims.quote: 57 minutes on thirteen refunds

value.unit: minutes of people's time in design C

claims.text: Design D, three policies, gets every case right in 18 minutes, because the rules decide where they can, mismatches are recorded rather than escalated, and the first damaged-but-kept case becomes a precedent.
claims.quote: Design D gets every case right in 18, because the rules decide where they can

value.unit: minutes of people's time in design D

claims.text: Refusing is not the same as being right: the $150 refund is refused, so the customer owed $120 gets nothing, and a control that refuses needs an owner for what it refused.
claims.quote: A control that refuses needs an owner for what it refused

claims.text: The right amount can come from the wrong decider: one case is paid exactly right, $261, as three refunds of $87 each under the limit, and only a decision policy that says who decides catches it.
claims.quote: Only a decision policy that says who decides catches it.

claims.text: He says adding another model to check the first is not necessarily enough, and that authoritative business rules or deterministic checks are a stronger basis; the twin's amount comes from a calculator the agent cannot change.
claims.quote: The amount is worked out by a calculator from the order records, which the agent cannot change.

claims.text: The twin answers his five questions: the agent can read the sender's orders and propose a refund but in design D only the workflow can pay, and intervention is a pause, a route up one altitude above $200, and a person for uncovered cases.
claims.quote: A pause on refunds for one order, a route up one altitude above $200, and a person for anything no rule covers.

claims.text: The evidence for removing the human is the case record: a person's decision becomes precedent P-1, matching cases follow it, a differing case is distinguished and escalates, and a precedent that holds is written into policy and then code.
claims.quote: The evidence for removing the human is the record of the cases where the human was there, and agreed.

claims.text: Who is accountable is the person who signed off the limit at that altitude: the head of support who signs the rules decide refunds up to $200 owns that sentence when the evidence turns out thin.
claims.quote: The head of support who signs "the rules decide refunds up to $200" owns that sentence

claims.text: His closing question should be put to a team in two halves: show me the cases, and show me who signed.
claims.quote: Show me the cases. And show me who signed.

claims.text: The twin is a simulation: synthetic orders, scripted mistakes, no real store and no model called; it shows how controls interact, not how often an agent makes each mistake.
claims.quote: Synthetic orders, scripted mistakes, no real store and no model called.

claims.text: The minutes are assumptions, six a case and three an approval; the comparison between designs matters more than the totals.
claims.quote: Six minutes a case and three an approval are mine; the comparison between designs matters more than the totals.

claims.text: Northstar is his: the retailer and the $120, $150 and $200 are from his article, and the other twelve cases are ours.
claims.quote: The retailer and the $120, $150 and $200 are from his article; the other twelve cases are ours.

claims.text: The mapping is ours: he presents the four questions as connected capabilities, not as a grid, and placing each control in a cell is our reading.
claims.quote: placing each control in a cell is our reading.

claims.text: The twin was built by this site's agent from his scenario in an sgit vault published with a public read key, and every number in the article is from its engine; the memo is from 18 October 2026.
claims.quote: every number above is from its engine.
